source_text: Ceterum quae ratio est, manibus quidem ablutis, spiritu uero sordente orationem obire, quando et ipsis manibus spiritales munditiae sint necessariae, ut a falso, a caede, a saeuitia, a ueneficiis, ab idololatria ceterisque maculis, quae spiritu conceptae manuum opera transiguntur, purae alleuentur? hae sunt uerae munditiae, non quas plerique superstitiose curant, ad omnem orationem, etiam cum a lauacro totius corporis ueniunt, aquam sumentes. id cum scrupulosius percontarer et rationem requirerem, comperi commemorationem esse Pilatum manus abluisse in domini deditione. nos dominum adoramus, non dedimus, immo et aduersari debemus deditoris exemplo nec propterea manus abluere. nisi ob aliquod conuersationis humanae inquinamentum conscientiae causa lauemus, ceterum satis mundae sunt manus, quas cum toto corpore in Christo semel lauimus.
thought_title: True cleanness of hands is spiritual, not ritual washing
orientation: Tertullian is arguing that the purity required for prayer is inward, not the superstitious washing of hands that some practice even after a full bath.
pass_a_gloss: But what reason is there, with hands indeed washed, but with the spirit being dirty, to go to prayer, when also for the hands themselves spiritual cleannesses are necessary, so that from falsehood, from murder, from cruelty, from poisonings, from idolatry and the other stains, which conceived in the spirit are carried out by the works of the hands, they may be lifted up pure? These are the true cleannesses, not those which most people superstitiously take care of, taking water for every prayer, even when they come from a bath of the whole body. When I was investigating this rather scrupulously and was seeking the reason, I found that it is a commemoration that Pilate washed his hands in the handing over of the Lord. We adore the Lord, we did not hand him over, indeed we ought also to oppose the example of the betrayer and not for that reason wash our hands. Unless on account of some defilement of human conduct we wash for the sake of conscience, otherwise the hands are clean enough, which we washed once with the whole body in Christ.

choices.english: but with the spirit being dirty
choices.why: Keeps the ablative absolute force and the contrast with washed hands; 'dirty' preserves the physical metaphor Tertullian is using for spiritual impurity.
Obeo means to go to or attend to; 'go to prayer' keeps the motion sense and the ritual context.
Plural 'cleannesses' preserves the Latin plural, which emphasizes the multiple kinds of purity required; 'spiritual' follows the glossary for spiritalis.
Sumentes is a participle of taking; 'taking water' keeps the action concrete and the participle force.

choices.english: in the handing over of the Lord
choices.why: Deditio is the act of handing over or surrender; 'handing over' preserves the betrayal sense without importing 'betrayal' which is a different Latin word.
rejected: in the surrender of the Lord

choices.why: Deditor is the one who hands over; 'betrayer' captures the negative moral force Tertullian attaches to Pilate's act.
rejected: the example of the one who handed him over

bible_refs.note: Pilate washing his hands in the handing over of the Lord (Pilatum manus abluisse in domini deditione)

pass_b_english: But what sense does it make to go to prayer with hands washed while the spirit is dirty, when the hands themselves need spiritual cleanness so that they may be lifted up pure from falsehood, murder, cruelty, poisoning, idolatry, and the other stains that are conceived in the spirit and carried out by the work of the hands? These are the true cleannesses, not the ones most people superstitiously fuss over by taking water before every prayer, even when they come from a bath of the whole body. When I investigated this rather carefully and asked for the reason, I found that it is a commemoration of Pilate washing his hands in the handing over of the Lord (Matthew 27:24). We worship the Lord; we do not hand him over. In fact, we ought to oppose the example of the betrayer and not wash our hands for that reason. Unless we wash them because of some defilement of human conduct for the sake of conscience, our hands are clean enough, since we washed them once for all with the whole body in Christ.
